fullPassage: It is difficult, if not impossible, to define the limits which reason should impose on the desire for wealth; for there is no absolute or definite amount of wealth which will satisfy a man. The amount is always relative, that is to say, just so much as will maintain the proportion between what he wants and what he gets; for to measure a man's happiness only by what he gets, and not also by what he expects to get, is as pointless as to try and express a fraction which shall have a numerator but no denominator. A man never feels the loss of things which it never occurs to him to ask for; he is just as happy without them; whilst another, who may have a hundred times as much, feels miserable because he has not got the one thing he wants. In fact, every man has a horizon of his own, and he will expect as much as he thinks it is possible for him to get. Sensory organs are the only channels of communication between the brain and the outside world. Simply put, the brain is not designed to sense on its own. For instance, an exposed brain would neither sense light shining on it nor feel something touching it. In fact, patients are often kept awake during brain surgery, which can help a surgeon isolate specific regions of the brain. The ancient Greek philosopher Aristotle recognized this characteristic of the brain over 2,000 years ago when he said, "Nothing is in the mind that does not pass through the senses." This concept can be seen clearly when volunteers are blind-folded and placed in the warm water of a sensory deprivation tank. They soon experience visual, auditory, and tactile (touch) hallucinations, as well as incoherent thought patterns. From these experiments and others, it is apparent that we need constant input from our senses to carry out functions that give us personality and intellect. Great scientists are seldom one-hit wonders. Newton is a prime example: beyond the Newtonian mechanics, he developed the theory of gravitation, calculus, laws of motion, and optimization. In fact, well-known scientists are often involved in multiple discoveries, a phenomenon potentially explained by the Matthew effect. Indeed, an initial success may offer a scientist legitimacy, improve peer perception, provide knowledge of how to score and win, enhance social status, and attract resources and quality collaborators, each of these payoffs further increasing her odds of scoring another win. Yet, there is an appealing alternative explanation: Great scientists have multiple hits and consistently succeed in their scientific endeavors simply because they're exceptionally talented. Therefore, future success again goes to those who have had success earlier, not because of advantages offered by the previous success, but because the earlier success was indicative of a hidden talent. The Matthew effect posits that success alone increases the future probability of success, raising the question: Does status dictate outcomes, or does it simply reflect an underlying talent or quality? In other words, is there really a Matthew effect after all? When we realize we've said something in error and we pause to go back to correct it, we stop gesturing a couple of hundred milliseconds before we stop speaking. Such sequences suggest the startling notion that our hands "know" what we're going to say before our conscious minds do, and in fact this is often the case. Gesture can mentally prime a word so that the right term comes to our lips. When people are prevented from gesturing, they talk less fluently: their speech becomes halting because their hands are no longer able to supply them with the next word, and the next. Not being able to gesture has other deleterious effects: without gesture to help our mental processes along, we remember less useful information, we solve problems less well, and we are less able to explain our thinking. Far from tagging along as speech's clumsy companion, gesture represents the leading edge of our thought. On our little world, light travels, for all practical purposes, instantaneously. If a lightbulb is glowing, then of course it's physically where we see it, shining away. We reach out our hand and touch it: It's there all right, and unpleasantly hot. If the filament fails, then the light goes out. We don't see it in the same place, glowing, illuminating the room years after the bulb breaks and it's removed from its socket. The very notion seems nonsensical. But if we're far enough away, an entire sun can go out and we'll continue to see it shining brightly: we won't learn of its death, it may be, for ages to come — in fact, for how long it takes light, which travels fast but not infinitely fast, to cross the intervening vastness. The immense distances to the stars and the galaxies mean that we see everything in space in the past. The big problem with money created by the government is that those who run the government always face the temptation to create more money and spend it. Whether among ancient kings or modern politicians, this has happened again and again over the centuries, leading to inflation and the many economic and social problems that follow from inflation. For this reason, many countries have preferred using gold, silver, or some other material that is inherently limited in supply, as money. It is a way of depriving governments of the power to expand the money supply to inflationary levels. Gold has long been considered ideal for this purpose, since the supply of gold in the world usually cannot be increased rapidly. When paper money is convertible into gold whenever the individual chooses to do so, then the money is said to be "backed up" by gold. This expression is misleading only if we imagine that the value of the gold is somehow transferred to the paper money, when in fact the real point is that the gold simply limits the amount of paper money that can be issued. As a general rule, it's better if your definition corresponds as closely as possible to the way in which the term is ordinarily used in the kinds of debates to which your claims are pertinent. There will be, however, occasions where it is appropriate, even necessary, to coin special uses through what philosophers call stipulative definition. This would be the case where the current lexicon is not able to make distinctions that you think are philosophically important. For example, we do not have a term in ordinary language that describes a memory that is not necessarily a memory of something the person having it has experienced. Such a thing would occur, for example, if I could somehow share your memories: I would have a memory-type experience, but this would not be of something that I had actually experienced. To call this a memory would be misleading. For this reason, philosophers have coined the special term 'quasi-memory' to refer to these hypothetical memory-like experiences. In 1900, at the close of the first decade in which electric systems had become a practical alternative for manufacturers, less than 5 percent of the power used in factories came from electricity. But the technological advances of suppliers made electric systems and electric motors ever more affordable and reliable, and the suppliers' intensive marketing programs also sped the adoption of the new technology. Further accelerating the shift was the rapid expansion in the number of skilled electrical engineers, who provided the expertise needed to install and run the new systems. In short order, electric power had gone from exotic to commonplace. But one thing didn't change. Factories continued to build their own power-supply systems on their own premises. Designed to supply lighting to local homes and shops, the central stations had neither the size nor the skill to serve the needs of big factories. And the factory owners, having always supplied their own power, were unwilling to assign such a critical function to an outsider. They knew that a glitch in power supply would bring their operations to a halt — and that a lot of glitches might well mean bankruptcy. If we're partial to one option — perhaps because it's more memorable, or framed to minimize loss, or seemingly consistent with a promising pattern — we tend to search for information that will justify choosing that option. On the one hand, it's sensible to make choices that we can defend with data and a list of reasons. On the other hand, if we're not careful, we're likely to conduct an imbalanced analysis, falling prey to a cluster of errors collectively known as "confirmation biases." For example, nearly all companies include classic "tell me about yourself" job interviews as part of the hiring process, and many rely on these interviews alone to evaluate applicants. But it turns out that traditional interviews are actually one of the least useful tools for predicting an employee's future success. This is because interviewers often subconsciously make up their minds about interviewees based on their first few moments of interaction and spend the rest of the interview cherry-picking evidence and phrasing their questions to confirm that initial impression: "I see here you left a good position at your previous job. You must be pretty ambitious, right?" versus "You must not have been very committed, huh?" This means that interviewers can be prone to missing significant information that would clearly indicate whether this candidate was actually the best person to hire. More structured approaches, like obtaining samples of a candidate's work or asking how he would respond to difficult hypothetical situations, are dramatically better at assessing future success, with a nearly threefold advantage over traditional interviews. The study of emotions and decision making is now of considerable importance. This involves the application of various tools afforded by neuroscience. One important stream of the literature examines people with brain damage and how damage to particular parts of the brain known to be responsible for particular cognitive functions impacts on decision making. One example of this research is the work of Antonio Damasio, who finds that when the emotional part of the brain is damaged, this actually reduces the efficacy of decision making. Good decisions are a product of the emotional part of the brain working in conjunction with the deliberative part. This contradicts the assumptions of conventional economics, where emotions play a negative role in the decision-making process. Here it is assumed that decision making can be modeled as being generated in a stoic, unemotional fashion, and that's why decisions tend to be optimal. But the evidence suggests that emotions actually play an important and, often, a positive role in decision making.

questions.stem: 다음 글의 빈칸에 들어갈 말로 가장 적절한 것은?

det.korean: 공장주들은 그렇게 중요한 기능을 '외부인(outsider)'에게 맡기기를 꺼렸다는 맥락
det.analysis:
❌ ① engineer — '기술자'. 뒤에 이어지는 정전 위험 논리와 달리, 특정 직군을 가리켜 문맥이 좁아짐
❌ ② customer — '고객'. 공장주가 전력을 '맡기는' 대상이 고객이라는 것은 어색함
✅ ③ outsider — '외부인'. 늘 자체 전력을 공급해 온 공장주들이 중요한 기능을 '외부인'에게 넘기기를 꺼렸다는 흐름에 정확히 부합 (바로 뒤 문장의 정전·파산 우려가 근거)
❌ ④ employee — '직원'. 내부 직원에게 맡기는 것은 꺼릴 이유가 약하므로 문맥과 맞지 않음
det.tip: unwilling to assign such a critical function to an outsider = 그런 중요한 기능을 외부인에게 맡기기를 꺼리는

questions.passage: We have biases that support our biases! If we're partial to one option — perhaps because it's more memorable, or framed to minimize loss, or seemingly consistent with a promising pattern — we tend to search for information that will __________ choosing that option. On the one hand, it's sensible to make choices that we can defend with data and a list of reasons. On the other hand, if we're not careful, we're likely to conduct an imbalanced analysis, falling prey to a cluster of errors collectively known as "confirmation biases." For example, nearly all companies include classic "tell me about yourself" job interviews as part of the hiring process, and many rely on these interviews alone to evaluate applicants. But it turns out that traditional interviews are actually one of the least useful tools for predicting an employee's future success. This is because interviewers often subconsciously make up their minds about interviewees based on their first few moments of interaction and spend the rest of the interview cherry-picking evidence and phrasing their questions to confirm that initial impression: "I see here you left a good position at your previous job. You must be pretty ambitious, right?" versus "You must not have been very committed, huh?" This means that interviewers can be prone to missing significant information that would clearly indicate whether this candidate was actually the best person to hire. More structured approaches, like obtaining samples of a candidate's work or asking how he would respond to difficult hypothetical situations, are dramatically better at assessing future success, with a nearly threefold advantage over traditional interviews.
questions.stem: 다음 글의 빈칸에 들어갈 말로 가장 적절한 것은?

det.korean: 우리는 선호하는 선택을 '정당화해(justify)' 줄 정보를 찾는 경향이 있다는 맥락
det.analysis:
❌ ① forbid — '금지하다'. 선호하는 선택을 '금지할' 정보를 찾는다는 것은 확증 편향 설명과 모순
✅ ② justify — '정당화하다'. 한 선택지를 선호하면 그 선택을 '정당화해' 줄 정보를 찾는 경향이 있다는 확증 편향의 정의에 정확히 부합
❌ ③ oppose — '반대하다'. 선호하는 선택을 '반대할' 정보를 찾는다는 것은 확증 편향 설명과 모순
❌ ④ conceal — '숨기다'. 정보를 '숨긴다'는 것은 정보를 '찾는다(search for)'는 앞부분과 논리적으로 어긋남
det.tip: search for information that will justify choosing that option = 그 선택을 정당화해 줄 정보를 찾다

questions.passage: It is difficult, if not impossible, to define the limits which reason should impose on the desire for wealth; for there is no absolute or definite amount of wealth which will satisfy a man. The amount is always relative, that is to say, just so much as will maintain the proportion between what he wants and what he gets; for to measure a man's happiness only by what he gets, and not also by what he expects to get, is as <u>pointless</u> as to try and express a fraction which shall have a numerator but no denominator. A man never feels the loss of things which it never occurs to him to ask for; he is just as happy without them; whilst another, who may have a hundred times as much, feels miserable because he has not got the one thing he wants. In fact, every man has a horizon of his own, and he will expect as much as he thinks it is possible for him to get.
questions.stem: 다음 글의 밑줄 친 pointless와 의미가 가장 가까운 것은?

det.korean: pointless = 무의미한, 헛된 → futile(헛된)
det.analysis:
❌ ① logical — '논리적인'. 무의미함과 무관한 속성
❌ ② essential — '필수적인'. 무의미함과 정반대 방향의 의미
❌ ③ obvious — '분명한'. 무의미함과 다른 개념
✅ ④ futile — '헛된, 소용없는'. 분자만 있고 분모가 없는 분수를 표현하려는 것만큼 '무의미하다(pointless)'는 맥락에 가장 가까운 동의어
det.tip: as pointless as to try and express a fraction ~ = ~만큼 무의미한 ≒ futile

questions.passage: Sensory organs are the only channels of communication between the brain and the outside world. Simply put, the brain is not designed to sense on its own. For instance, an exposed brain would neither sense light shining on it nor feel something touching it. In fact, patients are often kept awake during brain surgery, which can help a surgeon isolate specific regions of the brain. The ancient Greek philosopher Aristotle recognized this characteristic of the brain over 2,000 years ago when he said, "Nothing is in the mind that does not pass through the senses." This concept can be seen clearly when volunteers are blind-folded and placed in the warm water of a sensory deprivation tank. They soon experience visual, auditory, and tactile (touch) hallucinations, as well as <u>incoherent</u> thought patterns. From these experiments and others, it is apparent that we need constant input from our senses to carry out functions that give us personality and intellect.
questions.stem: 다음 글의 밑줄 친 incoherent와 의미가 가장 가까운 것은?

det.korean: incoherent = 일관성 없는, 두서없는 → disjointed(두서없는)
det.analysis:
❌ ① organized — '체계적인'. incoherent와 정반대
❌ ② rational — '이성적인'. 일관성 없음과는 다른 축의 의미
✅ ③ disjointed — '두서없는, 산만한'. 감각 차단 탱크에서 겪는 '일관성 없는(incoherent)' 사고 패턴과 의미가 가장 가까움
❌ ④ vivid — '생생한'. 사고의 선명함을 뜻해 일관성 없음과 무관
det.tip: incoherent thought patterns = 일관성 없는 사고 패턴 ≒ disjointed

questions.passage: On our little world, light travels, for all practical purposes, instantaneously. If a lightbulb is glowing, then of course it's physically where we see it, shining away. We reach out our hand and touch it: It's there all right, and unpleasantly hot. If the filament fails, then the light goes out. We don't see it in the same place, glowing, illuminating the room years after the bulb breaks and it's removed from its socket. The very notion seems nonsensical. But if we're far enough away, an entire sun can go out and we'll continue to see it shining brightly: we won't learn of its death, it may be, for ages to come — in fact, for how long it takes light, which travels fast but not infinitely fast, to cross the intervening <u>vastness</u>. The immense distances to the stars and the galaxies mean that we see everything in space in the past.
questions.stem: 다음 글의 밑줄 친 vastness와 의미가 가장 가까운 것은?

det.korean: vastness = 광대함 → immensity(광대함, 거대함)
det.analysis:
❌ ① silence — '고요'. 크기가 아니라 소리와 관련된 개념
✅ ② immensity — '광대함, 거대함'. 빛이 가로질러야 할 우주의 vastness(광대함)와 의미가 가장 가까움
❌ ③ emptiness — '공허함'. 비어 있음에 초점이 맞춰져 광대한 '크기'와는 다름
❌ ④ darkness — '어둠'. 밝기와 관련된 개념으로 크기와 무관
det.tip: the intervening vastness = 사이에 놓인 광대한 공간 ≒ immensity

questions.passage: In 1900, at the close of the first decade in which electric systems had become a practical alternative for manufacturers, less than 5 percent of the power used in factories came from electricity. But the technological advances of suppliers made electric systems and electric motors ever more affordable and <u>reliable</u>, and the suppliers' intensive marketing programs also sped the adoption of the new technology. Further accelerating the shift was the rapid expansion in the number of skilled electrical engineers, who provided the expertise needed to install and run the new systems. In short order, electric power had gone from exotic to commonplace. But one thing didn't change. Factories continued to build their own power-supply systems on their own premises. Few manufacturers considered buying electricity from the small central stations. Designed to supply lighting to local homes and shops, the central stations had neither the size nor the skill to serve the needs of big factories. And the factory owners, having always supplied their own power, were unwilling to assign such a critical function to an outsider. They knew that a glitch in power supply would bring their operations to a halt — and that a lot of glitches might well mean bankruptcy. As the new century began, a survey found that there were already 50,000 private electric plants in operation, far surpassing the 3,600 central stations.
questions.stem: 다음 글의 밑줄 친 reliable과 의미가 가장 반대인 것은?

det.korean: reliable = 믿을 수 있는 → 반의어 erratic(들쭉날쭉한, 불규칙한)
det.analysis:
❌ ① durable — '내구성 있는'. 오래간다는 뜻으로 reliable과 오히려 유사
❌ ② efficient — '효율적인'. 성능의 긍정적 속성으로 반대가 아님
❌ ③ flexible — '유연한'. 신뢰성과 무관한 속성
✅ ④ erratic — '변덕스러운, 불규칙한'. 늘 믿고 쓸 수 있는(reliable) 것과 반대로 예측 불가하게 작동함을 뜻해 반의어로 가장 적절
det.tip: affordable and reliable(믿을 수 있는) ↔ erratic(들쭉날쭉한)

questions.passage: The big problem with money created by the government is that those who run the government always face the temptation to create more money and spend it. Whether among ancient kings or modern politicians, this has happened again and again over the centuries, leading to inflation and the many economic and social problems that follow from inflation. For this reason, many countries have preferred using gold, silver, or some other material that is inherently limited in supply, as money. It is a way of depriving governments of the power to expand the money supply to inflationary levels. Gold has long been considered <u>ideal</u> for this purpose, since the supply of gold in the world usually cannot be increased rapidly. When paper money is convertible into gold whenever the individual chooses to do so, then the money is said to be "backed up" by gold. This expression is misleading only if we imagine that the value of the gold is somehow transferred to the paper money, when in fact the real point is that the gold simply limits the amount of paper money that can be issued.
questions.stem: 다음 글의 밑줄 친 ideal과 의미가 가장 반대인 것은?

det.korean: ideal = 이상적인 → 반의어 flawed(결함 있는)
det.analysis:
❌ ① superior — '우수한'. 이상적임과 유사한 긍정적 의미
✅ ② flawed — '결함 있는'. 이 목적에 '이상적인(ideal)' 것과 반대로 결점이 있음을 뜻하므로 반의어로 가장 적절
❌ ③ perfect — '완벽한'. ideal과 거의 동의어
❌ ④ essential — '필수적인'. 중요성을 뜻하며 이상성과는 다른 축의 개념
det.tip: Gold ~ considered ideal(이상적인) ↔ flawed(결함 있는)

questions.passage:
(A) We reach out our <u>hand</u> and touch it: It's there all right, and unpleasantly hot. If the filament fails, then the light goes out.
(B) On the one <u>hand</u>, it's sensible to make choices that we can defend with data and a list of reasons. On the other hand, if we're not careful, we're likely to conduct an imbalanced analysis.
questions.stem: (A)와 (B)의 밑줄 친 hand의 문맥상 의미로 가장 적절하게 짝지은 것은?

det.korean: (A) hand=신체의 손, (B) On the one hand=한편으로는(관점·측면)
det.analysis:
✅ ① (A) 손 / (B) 관점·측면: (A)는 '손을 뻗어 만진다'는 신체 부위의 손, (B) 'On the one hand ~ on the other hand'는 '한편으로는 ~ 다른 한편으로는'이라는 관점·측면을 나타내는 관용 표현이므로 정확
❌ ② (A) 도움 / (B) 손: (A)를 '도움(give a hand)'으로 보면 '뻗어서 만진다'는 문맥과 어긋남
❌ ③ (A) 손 / (B) 시곗바늘: (B)의 hand를 '시곗바늘'로 보면 관점 대조 구조와 무관
❌ ④ (A) 일손·인력 / (B) 박수: 두 문맥 모두와 맞지 않음
det.tip: reach out our hand(신체의 손) vs On the one hand(한편으로는, 관용구)

questions.stem: 다음 영영 풀이에 해당하는 단어로 가장 적절한 것은? "the state of being unable to pay the money that you owe"

det.korean: bankruptcy = 파산 (빚을 갚을 수 없는 상태)
det.analysis:
✅ ③ bankruptcy — '파산'. 빚진 돈을 갚을 수 없는 상태라는 영영 풀이에 정확히 대응 (본문: a lot of glitches might well mean bankruptcy)
❌ ① inflation — '인플레이션'. 물가가 오르는 현상으로 풀이와 무관
❌ ② legitimacy — '정당성'. 정당함·합법성을 뜻해 풀이와 무관
❌ ④ expertise — '전문 지식'. 숙련된 지식을 뜻해 풀이와 무관
det.tip: unable to pay the money you owe = 빚을 갚을 수 없는 상태 = bankruptcy(파산)

questions.passage: One important stream of the literature examines people with brain damage and how damage to particular parts of the brain known to be responsible for particular cognitive functions impacts on decision making. One example of this research is the work of Antonio Damasio, who finds that when the emotional part of the brain is damaged, this actually _____ the efficacy of decision making.
questions.stem: 다음 글의 빈칸에 괄호 안의 단어를 문맥과 어법에 맞는 형태로 바꿔 (영어로) 쓰시오. (reduce)

det.korean: 주어 this(단수)에 맞춰 현재시제 3인칭 단수형으로 → reduces
det.analysis:
주절의 주어 this는 3인칭 단수이고, 일반적 사실을 서술하는 현재시제이므로 동사 reduce는 -s를 붙인 reduces가 알맞다.

원문: 'this actually reduces the efficacy of decision making'

감정 영역이 손상되면 이것이 의사결정의 효율을 '떨어뜨린다'는 현재시제 진술이다.
det.tip: this(단수 주어) + 현재시제 → reduce + s = reduces

questions.passage: But the technological advances of suppliers made electric systems and electric motors ever more affordable and reliable, and the suppliers' intensive marketing programs also _____ the adoption of the new technology.
questions.stem: 다음 글의 빈칸에 괄호 안의 단어를 문맥과 어법에 맞는 형태로 바꿔 (영어로) 쓰시오. (speed)

det.korean: 앞의 made와 병렬을 이루는 과거시제 → sped (speed의 과거형)
det.analysis:
등위접속사 and로 앞 절의 made(과거)와 병렬을 이루므로 동사 speed도 과거형이어야 한다. speed의 과거형은 sped(또는 speeded)이다.

원문: 'the suppliers' intensive marketing programs also sped the adoption of the new technology'

공급자들의 집중 마케팅이 신기술 채택을 '앞당겼다'는 과거 사실 서술이다.
det.tip: made(과거)와 병렬 → speed의 과거형 sped

questions.passage: We have biases that support our biases! If we're partial to one option — perhaps because it's more memorable, or framed to minimize loss, or seemingly consistent with a promising pattern — we tend to search for information that will justify choosing that option. On the one hand, it's sensible to make choices that we can defend with data and a list of reasons. On the other hand, if we're not careful, we're likely to conduct an imbalanced analysis, falling prey to a cluster of errors collectively known as "confirmation biases." For example, nearly all companies include classic "tell me about yourself" job interviews as part of the hiring process, and many rely on these interviews alone to evaluate applicants. But it turns out that traditional interviews are actually one of the least useful tools for predicting an employee's future success. This is because interviewers often subconsciously make up their minds about interviewees based on their first few moments of interaction and spend the rest of the interview cherry-picking evidence and phrasing their questions to confirm that initial impression: "I see here you left a good position at your previous job. You must be pretty ambitious, right?" versus "You must not have been very committed, huh?" This means that interviewers can be prone to missing significant information that would clearly indicate whether this candidate was actually __________. More structured approaches, like obtaining samples of a candidate's work or asking how he would respond to difficult hypothetical situations, are dramatically better at assessing future success, with a nearly threefold advantage over traditional interviews.
questions.stem: 다음 글의 빈칸에 들어갈 말로 가장 적절한 것은?

det.korean: 전통 면접이 이 지원자가 '채용하기에 가장 적합한 사람'인지 알려 줄 중요 정보를 놓친다는 맥락
det.analysis:
✅ ① the best person to hire — '채용하기에 가장 적합한 사람'. 전통 면접이 이 지원자가 정말 채용에 적합한지를 명확히 보여 줄 중요 정보를 놓친다는 앞 문장(면접이 성공 예측에 가장 쓸모없는 도구)의 논지에 정확히 부합
❌ ② the highest paid manager — '가장 많이 받는 관리자'. 급여 수준은 채용 판단의 초점이 아님
❌ ③ the most talkative candidate — '가장 말 많은 지원자'. 수다스러움은 적합성 판단 기준이 아님
❌ ④ the easiest question to ask — '묻기 가장 쉬운 질문'. 지원자의 적합성과 무관한 내용
det.tip: information that would indicate whether this candidate was actually the best person to hire = 채용에 가장 적합한 사람인지 알려 줄 정보

questions.passage: Great scientists are seldom one-hit wonders. Newton is a prime example: beyond the Newtonian mechanics, he developed the theory of gravitation, calculus, laws of motion, and optimization. In fact, well-known scientists are often involved in multiple discoveries, a phenomenon potentially explained by the Matthew effect. Indeed, an initial success may offer a scientist legitimacy, improve peer perception, provide knowledge of how to score and win, enhance social status, and attract resources and quality collaborators, each of these payoffs further increasing her odds of scoring another win. Yet, there is an appealing alternative explanation: Great scientists have multiple hits and consistently succeed in their scientific endeavors simply because they're exceptionally talented. Therefore, future success again goes to those who have had success earlier, not because of advantages offered by the previous success, but because the earlier success was indicative of __________. The Matthew effect posits that success alone increases the future probability of success, raising the question: Does status dictate outcomes, or does it simply reflect an underlying talent or quality? In other words, is there really a Matthew effect after all?
questions.stem: 다음 글의 빈칸에 들어갈 말로 가장 적절한 것은?

det.korean: 이전 성공이 '숨은 재능'을 보여 주는 지표였기에 미래 성공으로 이어진다는 맥락
det.analysis:
❌ ① a random outcome — '무작위 결과'. 성공이 우연이라는 것은 재능 때문이라는 대안적 설명과 반대
❌ ② a social advantage — '사회적 이점'. 앞 절에서 '이전 성공이 준 이점 때문이 아니라(not because of advantages)'라고 명시적으로 부정함
❌ ③ a lucky accident — '운 좋은 우연'. 재능이 아니라 운이라는 뜻이라 논지와 반대
✅ ④ a hidden talent — '숨은 재능'. 이전 성공이 이점을 줘서가 아니라 '숨은 재능'을 보여 주는 지표였기 때문이라는 흐름(they're exceptionally talented)에 정확히 부합
det.tip: not because of advantages ~ but because the earlier success was indicative of a hidden talent = 이점 때문이 아니라 숨은 재능의 지표였기 때문
